title: Wave-Particle Duality and De Broglie Hypothesis
short_intro: Wave-particle duality posits that all material particles and electromagnetic radiation exhibit both wave and particle characteristics depending on the experimental context. The de Broglie hypothesis quantitatively links the momentum of a particle to its associated wavelength.

exam_scope.tgt_core: De Broglie wavelength formula, momentum and kinetic energy dependence, basic Davisson-Germer experiment concepts, and photoelectric effect fundamentals.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Relativistic de Broglie wavelength, phase and group velocities of matter waves, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle derivation from wave packets, and fine details of electron diffraction.

prerequisites: Classical mechanics of waves and particles

concept_notes.heading: De Broglie Hypothesis of Matter Waves
bullets: Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that moving material particles possess an associated wave nature, just like radiation.
The wavelength lambda associated with a particle of mass m moving with velocity v is given by lambda = h / (mv), where h is Planck's constant.
Matter waves are probability waves and do not require a physical medium for propagation.

concept_notes.heading: Davisson-Germer Experiment
bullets: First experimental confirmation of the wave nature of electrons through electron diffraction from a nickel single crystal.
Observed a sharp maximum in scattered electron intensity at an accelerating potential of 54 V and scattering angle of 50 degrees.
The measured wavelength matched precisely with the theoretical de Broglie wavelength calculated for 54 eV electrons.

concept_notes.heading: Phase Velocity and Group Velocity
bullets: A matter wave is represented as a wave packet rather than a single monochromatic wave, requiring the distinction between phase velocity (v<sub>p</sub>) and group velocity (v<sub>g</sub>).
The group velocity of the matter wave packet is equal to the classical particle velocity v (v<sub>g</sub> = v).
The phase velocity of matter waves exceeds the speed of light in vacuum (v<sub>p</sub> = c<sup>2</sup> / v > c), but carries no physical signal.

concept_notes.heading: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle as a Consequence
bullets: Wave-particle duality imposes an intrinsic limitation on the simultaneous measurement of conjugate variables.
The position-momentum uncertainty relation is given by Delta x Delta p >= h / (4 pi).
The time-energy uncertainty relation is given by Delta E Delta t >= h / (4 pi).

derivations.title: De Broglie Wavelength in Terms of Kinetic Energy and Accelerating Potential
derivations.conditions: Non-relativistic charged particle of mass m and charge q accelerated through potential V
steps: Start with the definition of de Broglie wavelength: lambda = h / p.
Express momentum p in terms of kinetic energy K: p = \sqrt{2mK}.
Substitute kinetic energy for a charged particle accelerated through potential V: K = qV, hence p = \sqrt{2mqV}.
Substitute p back into the wavelength equation to obtain lambda = h / \sqrt{2mqV}.

derivations.title: Relativistic De Broglie Wavelength
derivations.conditions: Particle moving at velocities comparable to the speed of light c
steps: Use the relativistic total energy relation E<sup>2</sup> = p<sup>2</sup>c<sup>2</sup> + m<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>c<sup>4</sup> and rest energy E<sub>0</sub> = m<sub>0</sub>c<sup>2</sup>.
Express momentum p as p = \frac{1}{c} \sqrt{E^2 - E_0^2} = \frac{1}{c} \sqrt{(K + m_0c^2)^2 - m_0^2c^4} = \frac{1}{c} \sqrt{K^2 + 2Km_0c^2}.
Substitute this relativistic momentum into the de Broglie relation lambda = h / p.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Davisson-Germer Experiment Polar Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Polar graph of scattered electron intensity versus scattering angle theta at a fixed accelerating potential (e.g., 54 V), showing a hump or spike at 50 degrees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The hump confirms constructive interference of electron waves scattered from different atomic planes of the Ni crystal, verifying wave behavior.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQs regarding diffraction peak angles and accelerating voltages.

graphs_and_experiments.title: De Broglie Wavelength vs 1 / \sqrt{V} Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a log-log or linear plot of lambda versus 1 / \sqrt{V}.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the inverse square-root dependence of de Broglie wavelength on accelerating potential for charged particles.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting slope to determine Planck's constant or charge-to-mass ratio.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wave Packet Envelope (Dispersion)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An amplitude-modulated wave packet showing a localized group of waves moving with velocity v<sub>g</sub> while individual phase ripples move at v<sub>p</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how a localized particle is constructed from a superposition of monochromatic matter waves with a narrow band of wave numbers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions distinguishing phase velocity from group velocity in advanced PGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V.
solution_steps: Use the simplified formula for electrons: lambda = 12.27 / \sqrt{V} Angstroms.

solved_numericals.question: Find the de Broglie wavelength of a proton of mass 1.67 x 10<sup>-27</sup> kg moving with a kinetic energy of 1 MeV.
solution_steps: Convert kinetic energy to joules: K = 1 \text{ MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}.

solved_numericals.question: An electron has a speed of 1.8 x 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. Calculate its relativistic de Broglie wavelength. (Given m<sub>0</sub> = 9.1 x 10<sup>-31</sup> kg, h = 6.63 x 10<sup>-34</sup> J s, c = 3 x 10<sup>8</sup> m/s)
solution_steps: Calculate the relativistic factor gamma = 1 / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 1 / \sqrt{1 - (1.8 \times 10^8 / 3 \times 10^8)^2} = 1 / \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 1 / \sqrt{0.64} = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25.
Calculate relativistic momentum p = \gamma m_0 v = 1.25 \times (9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}) \times (1.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}).

assumptions_and_limitations: De Broglie wavelength formula assumes a uniform isotropic medium and free particle behavior.
Macroscopic objects have imperceptibly small de Broglie wavelengths because Planck's constant h is extremely small, making wave properties undetectable in classical mechanics.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Matter waves are electromagnetic waves because they propagate in vacuum.
common_misconceptions.correct: Matter waves are probability waves (de Broglie waves), not electromagnetic waves, and do not involve oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
common_misconceptions.why: Electromagnetic waves are self-propagating transverse waves of electric and magnetic fields, whereas matter waves represent the probability amplitude of finding a particle.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The phase velocity of matter waves can transmit physical information faster than light.
common_misconceptions.correct: The phase velocity v<sub>p</sub> exceeds the speed of light, but the group velocity v<sub>g</sub> (which represents particle velocity) is always less than c.
common_misconceptions.why: Information and energy are transported by the wave packet at the group velocity, not the individual phase ripples.

quick_revision: De Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum: lambda = h / p.
Davisson-Germer experiment proved the wave nature of electrons through crystal diffraction.
Group velocity of matter waves equals the particle velocity (v<sub>g</sub> = v).
